passage:
Yogesh wanted a remote-control car that cost Rs 600. His weekly pocket money was Rs 50. He did the division on the back of his notebook: twelve weeks. It looked far, but it looked possible, so he kept going.

He asked his mother, Dolma, whether he could earn something extra. She said Rs 10 if he washed the family car every Sunday. Sunday after Sunday the jar filled faster, and the wait became shorter than twelve weeks.

Sarita also got money every week, and every day after school she stopped at the shop for chips and a sheet of stickers. Nobody added it up. After a month she tipped out the jar and found a few coins at the bottom, and no idea where the rest had gone.

Yogesh's patience wore thin in the sixth week. The car still seemed far. He wrote a new number on the jar: 200. When it reached 200, he did a little dance in the hallway. Then he wrote the next target underneath and kept going.

qa.q: How much did the remote-control car cost?
Why did Sarita's jar end up almost empty while Yogesh's kept filling?
qa.a: Sarita spent on chips and stickers and nobody added it up, while Yogesh worked out his weeks, earned extra on Sundays and set a smaller number on the jar when he felt discouraged.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling in the sixth week?
qa.a: Discouraged and impatient, because the car still seemed far away.
Sarita could keep a small tally of what she spends and set a goal with her weekly amount so she can see the finish line.

grounding: Four approaches to saving for a toy: dividing the price by weekly money, earning extra, spending on small things, and setting a smaller first target.
